section.title: Idolatry in the Temple
section.sectionRationale: Carried by the Spirit in a vision to Jerusalem, Ezekiel is shown four escalating abominations, each one closer to the heart of the temple than the last, the idol of jealousy, secret animal worship by the elders, women weeping for Tammuz, and finally men bowing to the sun with their backs to the LORD's own sanctuary. God's glory is present to see it all.
section.thesis: God shows Ezekiel that Jerusalem's true crisis is not Babylon's army but corrupted worship at the very heart of the temple, idolatry growing bolder and more brazen the closer it draws to God's own house, provoking Him to withdraw pity from a people who have already driven Him out in their hearts.
section.frameNote: Four scenes of escalating abomination: the idol of jealousy at the north gate; the seventy elders offering incense to carved images in darkness; the women weeping for Tammuz at the temple's north gate; and the twenty five men bowing to the sun with their backs to the LORD, provoking His judgment.

units.label: Carried in vision to the idol of jealousy
units.note: the glory already seen, now confronted with rivals

verses.text: In the sixth year, on the fifth day of the sixth month, I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me; and there the hand of the Lord GOD fell upon me.
Then I looked and saw a figure like that of a man. From His waist down His appearance was like fire, and from His waist up He was as bright as the gleam of amber.

He stretched out what looked like a hand and took me by the hair of my head. Then the Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and carried me in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the north gate of the inner court, where {{kanoh|the idol that provokes jealousy}} was seated.
And there I saw the glory of the God of Israel, like the vision I had seen in the plain.
“Son of man,” He said to me, “now lift up your eyes to the north.” So I lifted up my eyes to the north, and in the entrance north of the Altar Gate I saw this idol of jealousy.

“Son of man,” He said to me, “do you see what they are doing, the great {{toevah|abominations}} that the house of Israel is committing, to drive Me far from My sanctuary? Yet you will see even greater abominations.”

units.label: Seventy elders offering incense in the dark
units.note: the LORD does not see us, they say

verses.text: Then He brought me to the entrance to the court, and I looked and saw a hole in the wall.
“Son of man,” He told me, “dig through the wall.” So I dug through the wall and discovered a doorway.
Then He said to me, “Go in and see the wicked abominations they are committing here.”
So I went in and looked, and engraved all around the wall was every kind of crawling creature and detestable beast, along with all the idols of the house of Israel.
Before them stood seventy elders of the house of Israel, with Jaazaniah son of Shaphan standing among them. Each had a censer in his hand, and a fragrant cloud of incense was rising.

“Son of man,” He said to me, “do you see what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the darkness, each at the shrine of his own idol? For they are saying, ‘The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land.’”
Again, He told me, “You will see them committing even greater abominations.”

units.label: Women weeping for Tammuz
units.note: mourning a pagan god at the LORD's own gate

verses.text: Then He brought me to the entrance of the north gate of the house of the LORD, and I saw women sitting there, weeping for Tammuz.
“Son of man,” He said to me, “do you see this? Yet you will see even greater abominations than these.”

units.label: Backs to the temple, faces to the sun

verses.text: So He brought me to the inner court of the house of the LORD, and there at the entrance to the temple of the LORD, between the portico and the altar, were about twenty-five men with their backs to the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east; and they were bowing to the east in worship of the sun.

“Son of man,” He said to me, “do you see this? Is it not enough for the house of Judah to commit the abominations they are practicing here, that they must also fill the land with violence and continually provoke Me to anger? Look, they are even putting the branch to their nose!
Therefore I will respond with wrath. I will not look on them with pity, nor will I spare them. Although they shout loudly in My ears, I will not listen to them.”

toevah.gloss: Abomination, something detestable that violates covenant order, most often used of idolatry and the practices that accompany it. The word recurs through this chapter as each successive vision is announced as a greater toevah than the last, building the case for judgment.

kanoh.gloss: The idol of jealousy, an image so named because it provokes God's covenant jealousy, His right to His people's exclusive worship, comparable to a husband's jealousy over an unfaithful spouse. Its placement near the temple entrance itself is a direct affront to the LORD enthroned within.

basic.context: Sitting in his own house with the elders of Judah before him, Ezekiel is seized by a vision and carried by the Spirit to Jerusalem, to the temple itself. There God shows him, in ascending order of horror, exactly why judgment is coming: an idol provoking jealousy at the temple's own gate, seventy elders secretly worshiping carved images in a hidden chamber, women publicly weeping for the pagan god Tammuz at the LORD's own gate, and finally twenty-five men standing with their backs to the temple, faces turned east, bowing to the rising sun. God's glory, the same glory Ezekiel saw by the Kebar, is present through it all, watching what His own people do in His own house.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a Spirit-given vision of real spiritual realities happening in Jerusalem's temple, using a guided tour structure, each abomination revealed as worse than the last, to make an escalating case for judgment. Readers should take the sequence and its emphasis on nearness to God's presence seriously as the theological point, rather than treating every visual detail as an isolated puzzle to be solved apart from that overall movement toward the holy of holies.
basic.originalLanguages: Each scene is called a toevah, an abomination, a word bound up with covenant violation and idolatry throughout the Old Testament, and the chapter piles up abomination upon abomination to justify what follows. The very first idol seen is remembered as provoking God's jealousy, His rightful claim to exclusive worship from a people bound to Him like a spouse.
basic.typology: The elders who say 'the LORD does not see us' anticipate every generation that presumes on God's apparent silence as though it were absence, while the vision's movement ever closer to the temple's inner sanctuary anticipates the New Testament's warning that true worship must be guarded at its very center, not merely at its edges.
basic.christ: Jesus, cleansing the temple and grieving that His Father's house of prayer had become a den of thieves, stands in the same tradition as this vision, confronting corrupted worship at its source, and His own body becomes the true temple, cleansed and pure, in contrast to the defiled sanctuary Ezekiel is shown here.
basic.god: God is present to see every hidden abomination, even incense burned in a secret chamber the elders assumed was dark enough to hide from Him, and He is provoked to righteous jealousy precisely because His people were made for exclusive, wholehearted worship of Him alone. His judgment, withholding pity, answers a people who first withdrew their own hearts from Him.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 20:5 grounds God's jealousy in the second commandment against idols. John 2:13-17 shows Jesus cleansing the temple of corrupted worship in righteous anger. Romans 1:25 describes the same pattern, worshiping the creature rather than the Creator, seen here in sun worship at the temple gate.
basic.oneStory: This is the anatomy of the corruption that finally justifies the temple's destruction and the exile, a people who filled God's own house with rival gods while assuming He could not see, foreshadowing every heart that quietly enthrones idols while still claiming God's name, and pointing to Christ, who alone cleanses and makes His people a true temple of worship.

context.literary:
Chapter 8 is the first act of a single vision that runs to the end of chapter 11. It opens with a date and a transport, 8:1-3, and it closes with the Spirit carrying Ezekiel back to the exiles and his telling them what he saw, 11:24-25. Everything between is one continuous scene in the temple, and chapter 8 is the part that gives the reasons.

The act is built as a tour. A guide, the fiery figure of 8:2, leads Ezekiel from place to place and at each stop asks him a question: 'do you see what they are doing?' The question recurs at 8:6, 8:12, 8:15 and 8:17. Three times it is joined to a promise that something worse is coming, 8:6, 8:13 and 8:15, so the reader is led through a stair of increasing horror. The question matters because it answers the elders' slogan in verse 12, 'The LORD does not see us.' God, who is said not to see, is spending the whole chapter asking Ezekiel to look.

The movement is also from the outside in, and from the public to the hidden and back. The first idol sits at a gate where all could see it, 8:3-5. The second scene needs a hole in a wall and a second dig to reach a secret chamber, 8:7-12. The third shows women sitting at a north gate, in plain view, 8:14. The fourth is in the inner court between the portico and the altar, the most sacred space an ordinary worshipper could reach, 8:16. The tour ends not in a room but at an act, a gesture of backs turned to God.

The last two verses step back and summarize. Verse 17 adds violence to idolatry, tying the chapter to the 'crimes of bloodshed' of 7:23, and verse 18 announces the sentence that the chapters after will carry out: no pity, no sparing, and no hearing. The whole unit is the answer to the question a reader may ask at chapter 7: why is the end coming?
context.historical:
The vision is dated to the sixth year, sixth month, fifth day, 8:1, which is about 592 BC, some five or six years before Jerusalem fell in 586. The elders who sit before Ezekiel are the leaders of the exile community, as in 14:1 and 20:1, and they are there to hear from God. They are given something they did not ask for, the truth about the temple they left behind.

The abominations are drawn from a history. Ahaz had copied a Damascus altar and moved the bronze altar to one side, 2 Kings 16:10-16. Manasseh built altars to the host of heaven in both courts of the house of the LORD, 2 Kings 21:4-5, and set up a carved image in the house of God, 2 Chronicles 33:7. Josiah cleansed the temple of the vessels made for Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven, and removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun at the entrance of the house, 2 Kings 23:4-5 and 23:11. Josiah died in 609, and the evidence of Jeremiah and Ezekiel is that the old habits returned. Jeremiah complained that people stood in the house that bears God's name and said, 'We are delivered,' while they went on with all these abominations, Jeremiah 7:9-11, and that they set their abominations in the house, Jeremiah 32:34.

The cults described belong to a wider world. Judah had been a vassal of Babylon and sometimes courted Egypt. Egyptian religion honoured animal forms and the sun, and Babylon had its own sun god. Mourning for a dying and rising god of vegetation belonged to Mesopotamian religion, and the women who baked cakes for the Queen of Heaven in Jeremiah 7:18 show the same appetite for foreign devotion among ordinary households. The people were not abandoning their faith in Judah's God; they were adding everything else beside it.

The slogan in 8:12, 'the LORD has forsaken the land,' may reflect the shock of 597, when the king, the court and the best of the people were taken and the temple was stripped. Many in Jerusalem read the disaster as the failure of their God and went looking for others. The vision tells them they have misread it: the Lord had not left them, but they had left Him.

The leader named in 8:11 deserves a second look. Jaazaniah son of Shaphan belongs to a family on the side of reform. Shaphan the scribe served Josiah, 2 Kings 22:12, Shaphan's son Ahikam shielded Jeremiah, Jeremiah 26:24, and another son, Gemariah, had a chamber in the temple from which Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll, Jeremiah 36:10. A son of that household standing among the censers shows how far the corruption had reached, even into families that had once defended the word of God.
context.canonical:
The first commandment's concern with exclusive worship is the root. 'I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God,' Exodus 20:5, and Deuteronomy 4:15-19 forbids images in the form of any beast, bird or creature that crawls, and warns against bowing to the sun, moon and stars. The four scenes of Ezekiel 8 are a catalogue of exactly what that chapter forbade: an image, creeping things, a pagan mourning rite and sun worship. Deuteronomy 32:16 says they 'provoked His jealousy with foreign gods,' and Psalm 78:58 says they enraged Him with their high places.

The pattern of defilement in the temple runs through Kings and Chronicles, but the great turning point comes in this vision and the two that follow. In 9:6 the judgment begins at the sanctuary, with the elders who were before the temple. In 10:18-19 and 11:22-23 the glory of the LORD rises, leaves the threshold, stops at the east gate and then goes up from the city to stand over the mountain on the east. The abominations of chapter 8 are the stated cause of the departure.

The reverse is in chapter 43, where the glory returns from the east by the gate that faces east, 43:1-2, and God says the house will never again be defiled by its kings and their abominations, 43:7-9. The elders' question is answered by the return.

The New Testament draws the connections in several directions. Paul describes what happened in Romans 1:23, that people exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles, which is Ezekiel 8:10 turned into theology. He tells the church that it is God's temple and warns against idols in it, 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 and 2 Corinthians 6:16. Jesus drives the traders out of the temple with the words of Psalm 69:9, John 2:16-17. Revelation promises a city with no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted the exiles to know that their theology of disaster was wrong. If they believed that God was weak, or had gone, they would be tempted to join in the same worship their brothers at home were practising. He tells them what he saw so that they will understand why the end is coming and where the fault lies.

He also wanted them to see something about the nature of sin that the elders' slogan hides. The leaders say 'The LORD does not see us.' It is a lie told for comfort, because if God does not see, one may do what one likes in the dark. By showing that God sees, and that He even takes the prophet by the hair and shows him what is done in the dark, the vision breaks the lie.

There is a message for the exiles' own temptations too. They were not in Jerusalem and could not be accused of what the people there were doing. But the elders sitting before Ezekiel have the same idols in their hearts, 14:3, and the vision lets them know that the God they consult is not deceived. The warning to Judah at home is also a mirror for those abroad.

And Ezekiel wanted them to understand the cost to God. The phrase 'to drive Me far from My sanctuary,' 8:6, shows that the judgment that follows is not a petulant response but the end of a long process in which the people themselves drove out the God they had pledged to serve. When the glory leaves, the exiles are meant to see that He was driven out before He departed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what Ezekiel saw in a vision. Its details are not a catalogue of particular ancient practices that believers should watch for in order to avoid. Nobody today is likely to be bowing to the rising sun in the temple court, and treating the chapter as a checklist misses the pattern it teaches.

What the chapter does prescribe, by implication, is a way of reading the heart. Idolatry is not first about statues; it is about whom one thinks God to be and whether one believes He sees. The four scenes cover the object that provokes, the hidden chamber, the borrowed lament, and the posture of the back turned. Each has modern equivalents, but the passage does not give them. It gives a standard to measure by: whatever draws devotion away from the LORD, however secret, however religious in appearance, is what the text calls an abomination.

The chapter also does not endorse the elders' view that God has forsaken the land, even though that view is described. The text reports what they said and then corrects it, with God's seeing and God's questions. Believers are not to take quoted speech as the author's voice. The same applies to Tammuz: the passage describes the women weeping, without sanctioning it, and nothing in it suggests that mourning in itself is wrong, as long as it is directed to the LORD and not to false gods.

debates.question: Did these things actually take place in the temple, or is the vision symbolic?

views.label: Real events, seen by Ezekiel in vision
views.case: Ezekiel is carried 'in visions of God,' 8:3, and sees what is truly happening. The details are specific: a named leader, Jaazaniah son of Shaphan, a particular number of men, and places in the temple. The book later treats the elders' conduct as fact, 9:9, and Jeremiah accuses the people of the same abominations, Jeremiah 7:9-11 and 32:34.

views.label: A composite picture of Judah's sin
views.case: Some think the four scenes gather the worst of what had been done over decades, selected and arranged for effect. The animal engravings, the Tammuz rite and the sun worship are not recorded elsewhere as simultaneous practices, and the escalation looks literary. On this view the vision represents the whole truth about Judah's worship, even if each scene was not a single day's event.

views.label: Real, but not necessarily all at once
views.case: The vision shows what had been done in the temple precincts through those years and what was current in 592, without claiming that all four took place on one day or that they were open to every worshipper.

debates.bearing: The text claims to show what is happening, and the later oracles treat it as such. The sense of the passage does not depend on settling whether it is a single day's snapshot, since all views agree that Judah's worship had been thoroughly corrupted.

debates.question: Who was Tammuz, and what were the women doing?

views.label: A Mesopotamian god of vegetation, mourned in a yearly rite
views.case: The BSB footnote says Tammuz, meaning Sprout of Life, was a Sumerian god of fertility. The women are taking part in a seasonal lament for a god who dies and returns with the cycle of the crops. Tammuz is named only here in the Old Testament, which suggests the writer assumes his readers know the cult.

views.label: A wider symbol of foreign devotion
views.case: Whatever the detail of the myth, the scene says that a pagan figure was being publicly mourned at the gate of the LORD's house. The exact mythology matters less than the location and the openness.

views.label: A rite connected to household religion
views.case: Some suggest the scene belongs with the popular devotion of women in Judah to the Queen of Heaven, Jeremiah 7:18 and 44:17, which was also family-based and centred on food and offerings. The point is that women were not being singled out, since men also practised the sun worship and the elders the secret rites.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the women's weeping was for another god, at the LORD's own gate. The chapter's emphasis is on the place and the exclusivity of worship, not on the sex of the worshippers.

debates.question: What is the 'branch to their nose' of 8:17?

views.label: A pagan ritual gesture
views.case: The branch may have been held to the face in the sun cult, perhaps as an offering or a gesture of worship, which would link the line to the sun worshippers of 8:16.

views.label: A gesture of contempt toward God
views.case: The word for nose also means anger, and some read the line as an obscene or insulting gesture made at God, a final provocation after violence and idolatry. The verse stresses provoking God to anger just before it.

views.label: Obscure
views.case: The meaning of the phrase is not known. The Hebrew term for the branch is used of a vine shoot elsewhere, Numbers 13:23, but there is no parallel to the gesture, and honest interpreters note that the reference is lost to us.

debates.bearing: The verse is difficult and the safest course is to say so. Whatever the gesture was, the text places it as one more provocation after the violence of the land, and the sentence in verse 18 follows from the whole.

study.originalLanguages:
The vision opens with a figure whose appearance is a fire below the waist and 'the gleam of amber' above, 8:2. The Hebrew word for amber is chashmal, and the BSB footnote adds 'or as glowing metal.' It is a word that appears only in Ezekiel, here and in 1:4 and 1:27. The figure of fire and brightness is the same as the one seen by the Kebar River, and 8:4 says outright that the glory of the God of Israel is present 'like the vision I had seen in the plain.' Most readers take the guide to be the glory of God itself, in the likeness of a man.

The figure takes Ezekiel 'by the hair of my head,' 8:3. The word for the lock of hair is tsitsit, the very word later used for the tassels or fringes on Israelite garments in Numbers 15:38. It is a small point, but a picture of a lock, or tassel, gripped by a hand. The Spirit lifts him 'between earth and heaven' and carries him in 'visions of God,' the same phrase that opens the book in 1:1.

The idol of 8:3 and 8:5 is a semel, a rare word for an image, and it is one that provokes God to jealousy, a phrase that picks up the root of the 'jealous God' of Exodus 20:5.

In the second scene the walls are covered with 'every kind of crawling creature and detestable beast,' 8:10. The word for crawling creature is remes, the term Genesis 1 uses for the creeping things God made on the sixth day and put under human rule, Genesis 1:24-26. 'Detestable' translates sheqets, the word the law uses for unclean animals, Leviticus 11:10-13. Humanity, set over these creatures, is bowing to them. This is the same inversion Paul describes in Romans 1:23.

Each elder worships 'in the darkness, each at the shrine of his own idol,' 8:12. The Hebrew phrase behind 'shrine' is closely related to the word maskit, used of an engraved or carved figure, as in the 'sculpted stone' of Leviticus 26:1, and older English versions translate the phrase as 'chambers of his imagery.' The picture is of private, individual cults carried on in rooms inside the temple. The leader's name, Jaazaniah, means 'the LORD hears,' which sits uncomfortably beside the claim that the LORD does not see and the sentence that He will not listen, 8:18.

Tammuz, 8:14, appears in the Old Testament only here, and the women are described simply as sitting and weeping for him.

In 8:16 the men stand 'between the portico and the altar,' using the terms ulam and mizbeach, the porch of the temple and the altar of burnt offering, and 'with their backs to the temple of the LORD.' The temple door faced east, so facing east meant turning one's back on it, which is the gesture Jeremiah condemns in Jeremiah 2:27: 'they have turned their backs to Me and not their faces.'

Finally the 'branch,' zemorah, is a vine shoot, as in Numbers 13:23, and the word for 'nose,' af, also means anger. The line is uncertain, but the word can carry both senses.

typology.type: The idol of jealousy and the zeal of the true Son, Ezekiel 8:3-6
typology.fulfillment: An image provokes God's jealousy by occupying the place He alone should hold, and He says it drives Him from His sanctuary. When Jesus enters the temple and finds it a marketplace, His disciples remember the psalm, 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me,' John 2:16-17, quoting Psalm 69:9. The same jealousy for the Father's house that moved God in Ezekiel is now embodied in a Man with a whip of cords. The escalation is that the Son does not only announce the removal of the rivals; He gives His life to bring His people into the true house. The type falls short because Ezekiel can only see the abomination, while Jesus purges and becomes the temple.

typology.type: The hidden chamber in the dark, Ezekiel 8:7-12
typology.fulfillment: The elders think the dark conceals what they are doing and that God is not looking. Jesus says nothing concealed will not be disclosed, and what is whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed from the housetops, Luke 12:2-3, and Hebrews says that nothing in all creation is hidden from God's sight, Hebrews 4:13. In Revelation the risen Christ appears with eyes 'like a blazing fire' and says He is the One who searches minds and hearts, Revelation 1:14 and 2:23. The fiery figure who sees every chamber in Ezekiel's vision finds its fullest portrait in Christ, the Judge who sees. The pattern is of exposure leading to judgment, and the gospel's answer is that one can bring what is hidden into the light and be forgiven.

The men turn their backs on the temple to bow to the sun. Malachi promises that for those who fear God's name 'the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings,' Malachi 4:2, and Zechariah's song calls the coming of Christ the Dawn visiting us from on high, Luke 1:78. Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and the new Jerusalem has no need of sun or moon because the glory of God and the Lamb are its light, Revelation 21:23. The correspondence is of contrast. The created light that was worshipped is replaced by the light that made it. It is an echo, not a stated fulfilment, and the type falls short because it concerns a rejection, while the New Testament offers the true light.

typology.type: The defiled temple and the living one, Ezekiel 8:6
typology.fulfillment: The sanctuary fills with idols and God is driven from it. Paul asks the Corinthians, 'What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God,' 2 Corinthians 6:16, and Peter calls believers living stones built into a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:5. The house that was lost through idols is rebuilt from people, with Christ as its cornerstone, Ephesians 2:20-22. The escalation is that the temple is no longer a building one can lose; it is a people indwelt by the Spirit. The type falls short because the temple building could be filled with idols from the outside, while the new temple is guarded by the Spirit who lives within it.

study.christ:
This vision leads to Christ by contrast and by recognition. The contrast is between a temple full of idols and the One who is the true temple. The recognition is that the fiery figure of 8:2 is the One the New Testament presents as the one who sees all.

Begin with the figure himself. 'From His waist down His appearance was like fire, and from His waist up He was as bright as the gleam of amber,' 8:2. Ezekiel does not say whom he sees, but it is the same figure he met by the Kebar, enthroned, with the likeness of a man, 1:26-27. John saw the risen Christ in the same colours: eyes like blazing fire, feet like polished bronze refined in a furnace, and a voice like the roar of many waters, Revelation 1:13-15. In Ezekiel 43:2 the glory returns with a voice 'like the roar of many waters.' The New Testament does not reason its way to this link; it simply describes Jesus in the words of Ezekiel. The One who sees the elders' chamber is the One who says to the churches, 'I am the One who searches minds and hearts,' Revelation 2:23.

Then the question that opens the problem: 'The LORD does not see us.' Christ is God who sees. 'Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree,' He tells Nathanael, John 1:48, and the Gospels note that He knew what was in man, John 2:25. The point is not that this unnerves, though it does; it is that the One who sees everything is also the One who came to save. The gaze that Ezekiel's elders feared is the gaze of a Saviour.

The temple theme is the next link. The abominations drive the glory out of the house. In the gospel, the glory comes back, in person: 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory,' John 1:14, using language of tabernacling. Jesus cleanses the temple in the zeal of Psalm 69:9 and calls His own body the temple, John 2:19-21. Malachi had promised that the Lord would suddenly come to His temple and purify the sons of Levi like a refiner, Malachi 3:1-3. The cleansing that the elders refused to give themselves is given by Him.

Finally, there is the sentence that ends the chapter. 'Though they shout loudly in My ears, I will not listen,' 8:18. Jesus reverses that experience for those who come to Him, John 6:37. At the cross He bears the silence of the Father, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46, so that those who cry out in His name will be heard.

The warning is the usual one. The chapter is not a hidden portrait of the cross, and no scene should be turned into a code. The links are the figure of glory, the God who sees, and the temple that He rebuilds in His own body.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the one who sees. The elders' claim in 8:12 is the oldest excuse of the guilty, and the passage answers it with a question put four times to the prophet: 'do you see?' The same God who is accused of blindness leads a man by the hair into the hidden rooms. The psalmist asks how the One who planted the ear could fail to hear, or the One who formed the eye fail to see, Psalm 94:9. No dark room is dark to Him, Jeremiah 23:24, and Isaiah 29:15 pronounces a woe on those who think otherwise.

It shows a God who is jealous. The idol of 8:3 is called the idol that provokes jealousy, and jealousy here is not the pettiness of an insecure rival but the wrath of a husband whose home has been invaded. The law's description, 'a jealous God,' Exodus 20:5, and the song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32:16, are in view. Because He is a God of love, He cannot be indifferent to where His people give their love.

It shows a God who stays. His glory is present in 8:4, in the midst of these abominations. The text does not say that He had already gone; it says He is watching. Nothing in the chapter happens without Him there. This is patience, and the next chapters will show it giving way slowly: the glory moves to the threshold, 9:3, then to the east gate, 10:19, then leaves the city, 11:23. He does not abandon the temple in a moment. He is driven out, as 8:6 says, step by step.

It shows a God who explains Himself. Ezekiel is not told simply that judgment is coming. He is taken through the evidence, scene by scene, and asked what he thinks. The sentence of 8:18 follows a long hearing. That is a mark of a just judge: He does not condemn without showing the grounds.

It holds together tensions that sit uneasily. God is present, and yet He is driven from His sanctuary. He sees everything, and yet He asks questions. He is full of compassion, and yet He says 'I will not look on them with pity.' The resolution is that these are not contradictory moods but one character acting with integrity. His seeing is why His sentence is just. His presence is why the sin is so grave. His pity withdrawn is the answer to pity ignored. Even in this refusal, the God who says 'I will not listen' is the one who earlier said He would be a sanctuary for them in the nations, 11:16.

For worship, the chapter calls us to live before an open face. Secret religion, borrowed devotions and a back turned in prayer can all be done in the sight of the One who sees. The right response is not to hide, nor to blame the darkness, but to invite the searching look and pray as the psalmist does, 'Search me, O God, and know my heart,' Psalm 139:23.

crossReferences.note: The second commandment says God is jealous and forbids bowing to images. The idol of jealousy in Ezekiel 8:3-5 is the commandment broken at the very threshold of His house. Seeing the idol in the sanctuary shows how far the nation had moved from Sinai.

Moses warned against making an idol in the form of any beast, bird or creature that crawls, and against bowing to the sun, moon and stars. Ezekiel 8:10 and 8:16 are the same two warnings broken. The vision shows that every prohibition of the covenant had been trampled in the temple itself.

Manasseh built altars to the host of heaven in both courts of the house of the LORD. The practice in Ezekiel's vision has a precedent in the worst king's reign. Josiah's reform removed the objects, but the vision shows that the habit was not removed from the heart.

Josiah removed from the entrance to the house the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun. Sun devotion at the temple door was a known problem, and Ezekiel 8:16 shows that it had come back, with men now bowing in the court.

The wicked say, 'The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed.' It is the slogan the elders repeat in Ezekiel 8:12. The psalm goes on to ask how the One who formed the eye could not see, so the two texts together answer the excuse.

The Lord repeats the elders' slogans back to them, 'The LORD has forsaken the land; the LORD does not see,' and says the iniquity of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. It shows that chapter 8's accusations are the stated ground for the judgment in chapter 9, which begins at the sanctuary.

Jeremiah accuses the people of stealing, murdering and burning incense to Baal and then standing in the house called by God's name and saying, 'We are delivered.' He calls the house a den of robbers. Ezekiel's vision shows from inside the temple what Jeremiah condemned from the gate.

God says that they have turned their backs to Him and not their faces, yet in trouble they beg Him to rise up and save. Ezekiel's twenty-five men, standing with their backs to the temple, are the picture of this accusation in a single posture.

Paul says people exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds, animals and reptiles, and worshipped the creature rather than the Creator. Ezekiel's chamber of engraved creeping things and the sun worshippers in the court are two scenes of the exchange Paul describes.

Jesus drives out the traders and tells them not to make His Father's house a marketplace, and the disciples remember that zeal for the house will consume Him. The jealousy of God at the idol in Ezekiel's temple is now present in the Son.

What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? Paul answers that believers are the temple of the living God. The question is the one Ezekiel's vision raises, but now the temple is a people and the answer is separation from idols and the promise of God dwelling with them.

When the glory returns, God says the house of Israel will never again defile His name by their abominations, and tells them to remove them far from Him. It is the reversal of chapter 8. The same prophet who watched the glory driven out is shown the glory coming back.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God making a place for Himself among His creatures. Eden is a garden where He walks, 'in the cool of the day,' and the first sin drives the pair from His presence. The rest of the story is God's patient effort to dwell with people again. The tabernacle and the temple are the signs of that effort, and the glory that filled them, Exodus 40:34 and 1 Kings 8:10-11, is the sign that He has come. Ezekiel 8 is the moment the story's central hope is put at risk by the people it was meant to bless.

The chapter answers a question that has been building since Sinai. Israel was told 'You shall have no other gods before Me,' and was then given a house in which to meet God. The temple was meant to be the place where the first commandment was most perfectly kept. Instead it holds an image, engravings, a foreign lament and sun worship, and so the people have filled the dwelling of God with the very things the covenant forbade. The exile that follows is therefore not an accident of empires but the expulsion of a people who would not keep the house clean, and it is the same pattern as the expulsion from Eden.

The chapter sets up the departure of the glory, which is the saddest movement in the book, 10:18-19 and 11:22-23, and the later promise of its return, 43:1-5. Between them lie the new covenant, the new heart and the new Spirit, 36:25-27, which will make a clean dwelling possible. The Spirit who carried Ezekiel into the temple to show him its ruin will later be placed within the people themselves.

The story reaches its answer in Christ. He is the glory returning, 'we have seen His glory,' John 1:14, and the zeal that cleanses the house, John 2:17. He is also the one who promises that He and the Father will make their home with those who love Him, John 14:23. After the cross and the gift of the Spirit, the church is the temple, built of living stones, 1 Peter 2:5, and the vision's warning stands in force: God's people can still fill His house with rivals, 1 John 5:21.

The new creation ends the problem. Revelation 21 shows a city with no temple because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, 21:22, and nothing unclean or abominable will ever enter it, 21:27. The glory that left by the east gate is there in the midst of the people forever, and no one will turn a back on Him.

sermon.title: Corrupt Worship (Part 3)
sermon.why: Carson preaches through Ezekiel 8 and 9 together, tracing the escalating vision of idolatry in the temple that directly precedes and explains the judgment carried out by the six executioners and the departure of God's glory.

quiz.q: How was Ezekiel transported to see this vision of the temple?

options.text: He physically traveled by caravan from Babylon.
options.note: The transport is visionary, carried by the Spirit, not a literal journey.

options.text: A figure like a man seized him by the hair, and the Spirit carried him in visions of God to Jerusalem.
options.note: Ezekiel 8:2-3 describes this vivid means of transport in the vision.

options.text: He read about it in a letter from Jerusalem.
options.note: He is shown the scene directly in a vision, not through a letter.

options.text: The text does not describe how he arrived.
options.note: Verses 2-3 describe the means of transport explicitly.

quiz.q: What did the seventy elders say to justify their secret idolatry?

options.text: 'We are testing whether the idols have power.'
options.note: Their stated reasoning is about God's supposed absence, not an experiment.

options.text: They gave no explanation at all.
options.note: Their reasoning is quoted directly in verse 12.

options.text: 'The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land.'
options.note: Ezekiel 8:12 records this exact justification.

options.text: 'The LORD commanded us to worship these images.'
options.note: They do not claim divine command; they assume God cannot see them.

quiz.q: What were the women doing at the north gate of the LORD's house?

options.text: Celebrating a harvest festival.
options.note: The scene is specifically weeping for a pagan deity, Tammuz.

options.text: Offering grain sacrifices to the LORD.
options.note: Their mourning was for a foreign god, not a sacrifice to the LORD.

options.text: Praying for the exiles' return.
options.note: The text specifies mourning for Tammuz, not prayer for exiles.

options.text: Weeping for Tammuz, a pagan deity.
options.note: Ezekiel 8:14 states this plainly.

quiz.q: What was the final and greatest abomination Ezekiel was shown?

options.text: About twenty-five men with their backs to the temple, bowing to the sun in the east.
options.note: Ezekiel 8:16 describes this climactic scene at the temple's inner court.

options.text: Children playing in the temple courts.
options.note: The final vision is specifically sun worship, not children playing.

options.text: Priests offering the correct sacrifices at the altar.
options.note: The scene depicts sun worship with backs turned to the LORD, not proper sacrifice.

options.text: Nothing further is shown after the weeping women.
options.note: A fourth, climactic scene follows in verses 16-18.

quiz.q: What does God say He will do in response to these abominations?

options.text: Overlook the idolatry because of Israel's past faithfulness.
options.note: The text says the opposite; God will not spare or show pity.

options.text: Immediately restore the temple to purity.
options.note: The chapter announces coming wrath, not immediate restoration.

options.text: Respond with wrath, showing no pity and refusing to listen even when they cry loudly to Him.
options.note: Ezekiel 8:18 states this response directly.

options.text: Give no response at all.
options.note: God's response of wrath is stated explicitly in verse 18.

questions: The elders assumed 'the LORD does not see us' while sinning in what they thought was darkness. Where might you be tempted to act as though God is not watching or does not care?

Each abomination in this vision draws closer to the temple's inner sanctuary than the last. How does sin in your own life tend to escalate gradually, moving closer to what matters most, if left unchecked?
The men in the final scene had their backs to the temple while facing the sun. What are you facing toward this week, God or some substitute, even while claiming to belong to Him?

God's glory was present through this entire vision, watching idolatry unfold in His own house. How does knowing God sees everything, even what feels hidden, change the way you think about private sin?
Jesus later cleanses a corrupted temple with righteous anger. How does knowing that Christ takes true worship this seriously shape the way you approach your own worship and devotion to Him?

translationNotes.note: The idol that provokes jealousy, sometimes rendered image of jealousy, is not named more specifically in the text; scholars have proposed various Canaanite deities, though its precise identity remains uncertain.

Jaazaniah son of Shaphan is named individually among the seventy elders, possibly significant since Shaphan's family elsewhere in Scripture is associated with support for reform under King Josiah, making this figure's presence among the idolaters especially striking.
Putting the branch to their nose describes an obscure ritual gesture whose exact significance is debated among scholars, though it clearly forms part of the condemned pagan worship practice.
